analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts through independent citizen commissions instead of partisan legislatures.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from April 2024 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR MAPS Act would have required every state to draw its congressional districts through an independent commission of citizens — balanced between Democrats, Republicans, and independents — rather than by the party that controls the state legislature. It would ban mid-decade redistricting, forbid maps designed to unfairly favor one party, set objective criteria like keeping communities together, require public hearings and published data, and let courts and private citizens enforce the rules. It also would have applied to maps drawn after the 2020 census. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in April 2024 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states where legislators gerrymander congressional maps would get districts drawn by citizen commissions with no stake in the outcome, plus enforceable bans on partisan favoritism and mid-decade remapping. Voters whose communities are currently split across districts to weaken them would gain the most, since the bill prioritizes keeping communities together and protecting minority voting strength under the Voting Rights Act.

how_it_helps.text: It would require every state to draw congressional maps through a 15-member independent commission with membership balanced between the two major parties and independents, instead of letting legislators draw their own districts.
It would ban mid-decade redistricting, so parties could not redraw maps between censuses to lock in an advantage.

It would ban maps drawn to unduly favor or disfavor any political party, with violations measured using established fairness metrics, and would prohibit mapmakers from considering incumbents' homes or voters' party affiliation.

It would require open commission meetings, public hearings, published draft maps, public comment periods, and detailed written evaluations of each plan, and would give citizens and the Justice Department the right to sue to enforce the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities would lose their power to draw districts that protect their party and their own seats; taxpayers would fund state commissions through payments of $150,000 per congressional seat; and states would bear the administrative cost of building the commission system.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state law in every state, taking map-drawing power away from elected state legislatures and handing it to appointed commissions — critics view this as a federal overreach that removes accountability to voters.

The ban on favoring a party would be enforced using quantitative metrics like the efficiency gap and algorithmic comparison plans, which many scholars and courts have found legally fragile and contested, raising the risk of years of litigation over maps.

Compliance would be expensive and bureaucratic: 15-member commissions in every state, plus payments of $150,000 per congressional seat, for a process voters could perceive as removed from democratic control.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If it had passed, the benefit would have been fairer, more competitive House districts and less incentive for extreme gerrymandering, at the cost of federal preemption of state map-drawing power, a heavy administrative burden on states, litigation risk around quantitative partisan-fairness tests, and the objection that Congress cannot force state legislatures to give up this power. The bill's death preserved the current system, in which partisan map-drawing remains legal in most states.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and no committee or floor action ever followed before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wiley Nickel introduced the FAIR MAPS Act on April 9, 2024, with Rep. Zoe Lofgren as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which is the only committee action in its history.

No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, which means the bill died under congressional rules that require bills to pass both chambers within the same two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and whichever party controls each state's map-drawing process are better off, because they keep the power to draw congressional districts to their own advantage.

for.name: Rep. Wiley Nickel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 9, 2024 and delivered introductory remarks on April 29, 2024.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without scheduling a hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Set the House agenda and never brought the bill to the floor; as the party that benefits from gerrymandered maps in many states, it had strong institutional reason to keep map-drawing power with legislatures.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and it died in a committee controlled by the opposing party without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators
industries.note: The bill removes their power to draw their own districts and bans mid-decade remapping, directly threatening safe seats and party control of House seats.
Parties lose the ability to entrench House majorities through map-drawing, though redistricting litigation and consulting work would continue under new commission-based rules.

industries.industry: Voters and minority communities protected by the Voting Rights Act
industries.note: The bill's criteria prioritize protecting communities of interest and the ability of racial and language minorities to elect representatives of choice, and require public hearings and published data.
